title: base.hurry: mod_base_upkeep calls mod_base_hurry directly, bypassing the observer
description:
Found while analysing na-alr.2. Needs a real game to settle, so it is filed rather than fixed.

The base.hurry surface is intercepted by re-pointing ONE patch-table entry:

  patch.cpp:696   write_call(0x4F7A38, (int)na_base_hurry_observed); // base_upkeep

0x4F7A38 is a call site inside the ENGINE's base_upkeep. But Thinker also replaces base_upkeep wholesale on the production path:

  patch.cpp:693   write_call(0x527039, (int)mod_base_upkeep); // production_phase

and mod_base_upkeep (base.cpp:4248, 'Main base production management function during production_phase') calls the unwrapped function directly:

  base.cpp:4263   mod_base_hurry();

Every other caller of mod_base_hurry is inside our own wrapper chain — build.cpp:69 and :74 are na_base_hurry_observed's own stand-down paths, neural.cpp:3337 and :3408 are na_decide_base_hurry's. base.cpp:4263 is the only one that is not, and it sits on the main per-turn production path.

Two readings, and they need different fixes:
  (a) The engine's base_upkeep is dead on the production path, so 0x4F7A38 rarely or never fires and base.hurry decisions are mostly NOT routed to the brain. Fix: point base.cpp:4263 at na_base_hurry_observed.
  (b) Both paths are live, so some base-turns are observed and some are not, silently. Fix: same, plus check for double-counting against call_seq.

Evidence that does not settle it either way: upstream Thinker installs the 0x4F7A38 patch itself (it pointed at mod_base_hurry before we re-pointed it), and upstream would not patch a dead site — but docs/directives.md:181 cites a real turn-35 base.hurry observation, so the observed path demonstrably fires at least sometimes.

What would settle it: one instrumented run counting entries to na_base_hurry_observed against entries to mod_base_hurry. That is a game-fixture job (na-dyt / na-ie9), which is why this is filed rather than fixed here.

Related: na-04v is a paid grounding eval for exactly this surface. Worth settling this first — an eval over a surface that only fires on some code paths measures something other than what it claims to.
acceptance_criteria: The count of na_base_hurry_observed entries vs mod_base_hurry entries is measured in one real run; if base.cpp:4263 bypasses the observer it is re-pointed; any double-count against call_seq is ruled out.
notes: TRIAGE 2026-08-22 (Claude, remote session): still open and still needs exactly what it says — a live game to settle reading (a) vs (b), then the one-line thinker patch (point base.cpp:4263 at na_base_hurry_observed) with a call_seq double-count check. Adapter-side work in scbrown/thinker plus a running terranx.exe; neither exists in this container. Worth noting for whoever settles it: the na-qu8 eval run (2026-08-22) exercised base.hurry from a committed capture, not from the live path, so it says nothing about whether 0x4F7A38 fires in production.
close_reason: Reading (a), measured: before raw=136 observed=0 upkeep=136; after raw=0 observed=136 upkeep=136; double=0 both. Corroborated by the 2026-08-21 session log (324 base.production, 0 base.hurry). Root cause: base.production is hooked INSIDE mod_base_build so every caller reaches it, while base.hurry is wrapped and mod_base_upkeep called the raw function. Fixed in thinker 7a930f8 (base.cpp:4263 -> na_base_hurry_observed); 136 base.hurry decisions now reach the orchestrator where the previous session produced zero. hurry-stats census kept.

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## Settled by census, fixed, and verified in a live run — thinker `7a930f8` on origin/master (harding)

The bead asks for exactly one thing: *"The count of na_base_hurry_observed entries vs
mod_base_hurry entries is measured in one real run."* Measured, on a real save resumed at turn
101, one full six-faction round, on an **isolated copy of the game** so the live session was
never touched:

| | raw | observed | upkeep | double |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **before** | 136 | **0** | 136 | 0 |
| **after** | 0 | **136** | 136 | 0 |

`raw` counts entries to `mod_base_hurry` from anywhere and it is the **control**: a run where it
read 0 beforehand would have measured nothing at all, and `observed=0 upkeep=0` would have read
as "no bypass". 136 hurry decisions, every one through the unwatched door, none through the
patched one.

**This is reading (a), unambiguously** — not (b). The engine's own `base_upkeep` is dead on the
production path; there is no silent mixture. `double=0` both before and after, so the
double-count concern is measured rather than argued.

### Independent corroboration, from the other end of the pipe

The 2026-08-21 live session's decision log — 339 records, six factions, three turns:

    base.production 324   faction.se 13   faction.tech 2   base.hurry 0

The 324 is that measurement's own positive control. The pipeline works; this surface simply
never arrives on it. Two instruments, opposite ends, same answer.

### Root cause, and it generalises

`base.production` is intercepted **inside** the function it hooks — `mod_base_build` calls
`na_decide_base_production` at `base.cpp:1313` — so it is reached from every caller.
`base.hurry` is **wrapped** instead, and correctly so: `mod_base_hurry` has five return points
and spends through `hurry_item()` on its way out, so there is no point inside it at which a
different answer can still be given. The build.cpp comment already says this and it is right.

But a wrapper's coverage is a property of its CALLERS, and `mod_base_upkeep` — Thinker's
wholesale replacement for `base_upkeep` on the production path — called the raw function.
Re-pointing `0x4F7A38` covered the engine's copy, which production does not use.

So the defect was never the wrapper. It was that nothing checked who called it. Worth carrying
to na-yd4's 23 remaining surfaces: **for a wrapped surface, "the hook is installed" and "the
hook is on the path" are different claims**, and only the second one is worth anything.

### The fix, and what it produced

`base.cpp:4263` now calls `na_base_hurry_observed()`. Verified end-to-end by rerunning the same
save against a scripted-brain orchestrator:

    surfaces: base.hurry 136, base.production 33, faction.se 3
    base.hurry tiers: {'llm': 136}

**136 base.hurry decisions reached the orchestrator, where the whole previous session produced
zero.** `raw=0` afterwards is the wrapper never falling through: every one was routed.

### Two things this changes that are worth saying out loud

- **na-04v's paid eval was run on a surface the game was not asking about.** It is not
  invalidated — it measured prompt behaviour from a committed capture, not routing — but
  anything inferred about base.hurry *in play* from before this change concerns a decision
  nobody was ever offered. The bead predicted this ("an eval over a surface that only fires on
  some code paths measures something other than what it claims to"); it was worse than that,
  since the surface fired on no code path.
- **A base.hurry decision record carries `native_choice: null`, and always will.**
  `na_build_base_hurry` emits it only when `native_hurried >= 0` — the observation path — and a
  hurry cannot be both observed and decided, because the engine's version decides and spends in
  one pass. So **na-6db has no native baseline for this surface** and na-yd4's "native_choice is
  mandatory" rule cannot hold here. Pre-existing and by design, not introduced by this change,
  but it is now load-bearing because the surface actually fires.

### The instrument stays: `hurry-stats`

Over the command channel, in `dialog-stats`' idiom. Counters rather than log records — this
fires on every base every turn and per-call records would drown the log they exist to be checked
against.

It stays because it is what turned *"the surface is quiet"* into *"the surface is unreachable"*.
Those are indistinguishable in a decision log: a hurry that bypassed the observer writes nothing,
and so does a hurry that never happened. No amount of reading the log separates them.
`double` stays for the same reason in the other direction — after this change, the same base
reaching both doors in one turn is precisely what would produce two decisions for one hurry.

Seam manifest regenerated; na-alr.1's guard caught all four new seams unprompted, which is the
guard doing its job. 40 wire checks, 3 failures — **all three pre-existing**, confirmed by
stashing the change and re-running to the same count.

title: CI job building against upstream Thinker master
description:
v5.5 was six commits and +5163/-2190 by the time we looked. The turn-loop extraction would have been a much smaller thing to absorb at commit one than at commit six, and nothing told us it had happened.

A scheduled job that merges upstream/master into our branch in a scratch worktree and runs the develop build plus tests/run-na-tests.sh. It does not have to push or resolve anything — it only has to answer 'would this still build', and say so loudly when the answer changes.

The build is cheap enough to make this easy: 25 seconds from clean on 8 cores, with the full mingw32 toolchain and Wine already available in the container. The wire tests need no game.

Pair it with na-alr.1: once the seam guard exists, this job also answers the more interesting question — would a merge silently drop a seam — which is the failure the build alone cannot see.
acceptance_criteria: A scheduled CI job that trial-merges upstream/master, builds, runs the wire tests and (once na-alr.1 lands) the seam guard, and reports failure distinguishably from a merge conflict.
close_reason: Two things, and the second was a live bug. Added .github/workflows/upstream-drift.yml to the fork (its first CI): weekly trial-merge of induktio/thinker, seam checks BEFORE the toolchain install since they need nothing and catch what a compiler cannot, then a full ninja-develop build; a conflicted merge stops early rather than building a tree with markers in it. Verified the exact preset locally — exit 0, zero warnings, 32-bit PE DLL. ALSO FIXED: NeuralAmplifier's own ci.yml pinned scbrown/thinker at ref claude/neural-amplifier-smac-testing-uq1fcg, which stopped moving 2026-07-29 while master went on to f10683f — so the thinker-dll job had spent weeks reporting green for an adapter nobody runs. Now builds master.

title: Collapse the NA config footprint in main.h and main.cpp
description:
Two blocks carry most of our presence in these files, and both are pure additions today (so they are not causing conflicts yet) — but they are large enough that any upstream reshuffle of struct Config or option_handler turns them into one.

  main.h      188 added lines inside struct Config (plus 17 near VideoMode, 46 externs)
  main.cpp     50 added lines as a MATCH() chain inside option_handler

Both collapse to one line each:
  - struct Config gains 'NaConfig na;' with the 23 llm_*/na_* fields moving to our own na_config.h
  - option_handler gains 'if (na_option_handler(cf, name, value)) return 1;' before its fallthrough

That takes ~410 lines of presence in upstream-owned files down to about five, and puts the fields somewhere upstream will never touch.

The cost is real and should be weighed rather than waved through: conf.na_x becomes conf.na.x at roughly 88 call sites plus neural.cpp. Mechanical, but broad, and it makes one large mostly-uninteresting diff. Worth doing on its own commit, and worth doing AFTER na-alr.1 so the seam guard is watching while the call sites get rewritten.

Verify the parse path end to end afterwards, the way na-15o.4 did: v5.5 left option_handler as thinker.ini's parser, and the failure mode if that breaks is silent — every NA option reverts to its default and llm_factions=0 means 'no bridge in the loop', which looks exactly like a working build.
acceptance_criteria: All 23 llm_*/na_* options live in na_config.h and parse through a single delegating call; main.h and main.cpp carry no more than a handful of NA lines between them; all 23 options traced as still parsing from thinker.ini; build clean, wire tests green.
close_reason: main.h NA footprint 251 added lines -> 9; main.cpp 159 -> 116 (the 50-line MATCH chain is now one delegating call). New src/na_config.h holds struct NaConfig, the NaExitCode enum and the five NA externs; 71 access sites renamed to conf.na.<field> with the na_ prefix dropped to avoid stutter. thinker.ini KEYS deliberately unchanged — they are a user-facing contract and renaming them would silently reset every option to its default. Key->field mapping is now a table in neural.cpp rather than fifty else-ifs. Justified by measurement first: main.h is touched by 244 of upstream's 435 commits (56%). Because a broken parse is silent, added tests/check_na_options.py holding fields/table/thinker.ini to each other, with three distinct failure messages; verified it fails by deleting a table row. Build clean zero warnings, full suite green. Commit on claude/thinker-upstream-sync-us8srt.

title: Refresh the adapter notes' file:line citations for v5.5
description:
NeuralAmplifier's docs/thinker-adapter-notes.md is explicitly a source-grounded document — 'Verified against the fork at scbrown/thinker (paths are src/...; file:line cited)'. v5.5 invalidates a good part of it, and a stale citation in a document that advertises its groundedness is worse than no citation.

Known-wrong after the merge:
  - §2 injection-seams table: mod_faction_upkeep 'game.cpp:1557 (hook patch.cpp:511)' -> faction_upkeep in gameturn.cpp, and it is now a write_jump at 0x527290, not a write_call. The 'turn (whole faction)' row is the cleanest-handoff row, so it is the one most likely to be read and trusted.
  - §4 'The per-faction AI turn': the whole pipeline is cited as game.cpp:1561-1604 and names mod_production_phase / mod_social_ai / mod_allocate_energy. The sequence is upstream's to define and may itself have changed in the rewrite — re-read gameturn.cpp rather than just renaming the symbols.
  - §5.0 Mode B+ gaps: 'mod_allocate_energy returns early for humans (game.cpp:1908)' and the AI heuristic at 'game.cpp:1922-2010'. Both moved to gameturn.cpp; re-check the early return still exists before restating it as a gap the LLM tier must own.
  - The Mode B+ status note cites branch claude/neural-amplifier-smac-testing-uq1fcg, which no longer exists on origin (origin has master only). Point it at what is actually there.

Re-verify each citation against the merged tree instead of translating names mechanically — the point of the document is that a reader can open the file and find the thing.
acceptance_criteria: Every file:line in thinker-adapter-notes.md resolves in the merged fork; the faction_upkeep row records write_jump/0x527290; the dead branch reference is replaced; committed to NeuralAmplifier on claude/thinker-upstream-sync-us8srt.
close_reason: All 56 file:line citations re-resolved against the merged tree and verified to land on the right construct (scripted check: every citation printed and inspected). Highlights: the §2 turn row now reads faction_upkeep gameturn.cpp:1568, hook patch.cpp:516, and records that it became a write_jump(0x527290) whole-function replacement rather than a call intercept — which is why the seam must be inside the body. §4's pipeline re-read from v5.5 rather than renamed: init_save_game is new and runs first, and the strategy/energy/diplomacy half sits behind a full_game_turn() gate worth not glossing. §5.0's two Mode B+ gaps re-confirmed as still real (allocate_energy's human early return at gameturn.cpp:1971; mod_social_ai's at faction.cpp:1505-1507). Dead branch reference replaced. Also corrected §8: mod_base_reset is hooked at TWENTY sites (patch.cpp:883-902), not eleven — that citation was already stale before this sync, so the note says so and leaves the measurement it supports intact. just docs lint and just check both green.

title: Confirm NA config options survive upstream's config.cpp rewrite
description:
Upstream rewrote src/config.cpp (+238/-…) and touched config.h (+20) and main.h (+14). Our fork carries ~254 lines of main.h Config fields and a MATCH() chain in main.cpp's option_handler for llm_factions, llm_endpoint, llm_timeout_ms and the na_*_policy / na_endgame_observe / na_dialog_observe family.

The merge reports no conflict in config.cpp or main.h, which is exactly the case worth checking rather than trusting: if upstream moved option parsing out of main.cpp's option_handler into config.cpp, our MATCH() chain would still compile and simply never be consulted — a silent regression that turns every NA option into its default. llm_factions defaulting to 0 means 'stock Thinker, no bridge', so the failure looks like a working build that quietly stops routing decisions.

Verify by reading, not by assuming: confirm option_handler is still the parser upstream feeds thinker.ini to, and that our fields still land on the same Config struct upstream now populates.

Also reconcile docs/thinker.ini: ours is +402 lines documenting the NA options at point of use, upstream added 5 of its own for v5.5. Both sets belong in the merged file.
acceptance_criteria: Every llm_*/na_* option still parses from thinker.ini into conf (traced through the actual post-merge call path, not inferred); docs/thinker.ini contains both our 402 lines of NA documentation and upstream's 5 new v5.5 options.
close_reason: Traced, not assumed: v5.5's config.cpp rewrite does no ini parsing (no ini_parse/MATCH in it). main.cpp:645/651 still feed thinker.ini and thinker_user.ini to option_handler, and all 23 llm_*/na_* MATCH entries sit inside its body (main.cpp:21-448). docs/thinker.ini carries both our 22 NA option blocks and upstream's new faction_pair. Gap found and split out as na-15o.7: llm_timeout_ms parses but has never been documented in thinker.ini — pre-existing, not a merge regression (confirmed absent on master too).

title: base.retool already has a deterministic tier — it needs instrumenting, not building
description:
FINDING 2026-08-16, reading scbrown/thinker at 0028451. na-2mn lists base.retool among the 21 surfaces needing a deterministic tier built FIRST. For base.retool that step is already done, folded into select_build, and the epic's plan for this one surface should change accordingly.

Evidence, all in the fork:

- build.cpp:12 check_retool(base) — true only when a penalty would actually apply: plr_owner, difficulty > DIFF_SPECIALIST, retool_penalty_prod_change set, retool_exemption != RETOOL_ALWAYS_FREE, production not done, minerals_accumulated > retool_exemption.
- build.cpp:856-860 select_build calls it under 'if (base->plr_owner())' and sets retool = mod_base_making(prev_id, base_id) — the retool CATEGORY of what is currently being built.
- build.cpp:31 has_retool(base_id, item_id, retool) — whether a candidate falls in a different category.
- build.cpp:840 push_item applies score -= 400, or -800 when the current item is a secret project, to every candidate that would cross a category.

So the engine-side answer exists and is conservative in the right direction: when banked minerals are at risk, the chooser is biased toward finishing what it started, more strongly for a project. That is exactly what a deterministic tier for this surface would have been asked to do, and it covers precisely the case where the surface exists at all — the penalty is player-owned-base only (game-surface.md 3.1 already records 'penalty applies to humans only', base.cpp:1045, build.cpp:11).

What is genuinely missing is INSTRUMENTATION. grep -i retool src/neural.cpp finds only prose in the base.production effects note (neural.cpp:391) — no surface_id, no world view, no decision record. So base.retool is invisible: coverage cannot see it, and na-6db has nothing to A/B against even though a baseline exists.

Proposed re-scope of this surface within na-2mn: move it out of 'needs a deterministic tier' and into the instrument-then-observe track alongside the 26 ready surfaces (na-yd4). The work is an observation hook at the select_build retool branch emitting the surface with prev_id, the chosen item, both retool categories and minerals_accumulated — plus a side-effect-free probe, since a retool decision fires rarely and is otherwise unverifiable without playing until it happens.

NOT DONE HERE deliberately: the epic's own rule is 'one surface, one config flag, one probe, one coverage-table row', and the probe is what makes it verifiable. Writing the hook blind, with no SMAC install in this environment to fire it against, would produce exactly the unverifiable change that rule exists to prevent.
notes:
AUDIT OF THE OTHER 13, done in the same pass so nobody repeats it (scbrown/thinker @ 0028451).

base.retool is the OUTLIER, not the first of a pattern. The epic's premise holds for every other uninstrumented NO_AI_PATH surface I checked:

- unit.tectonic / unit.fungal / unit.patrol / unit.gift: the engine's action functions exist as raw address bindings in engine.cpp (action_tectonic 0x4CE210, action_fungal 0x4CE790, action_patrol 0x4CDA30, make_gift 0x547C10) and nothing in Thinker calls them for an AI faction. Matches game-surface.md 4 item 7 exactly.
- council.vote / council.buy_vote / diplo.treaty_offer / diplo.surrender: same shape — council_votes 0x52AD30, buy_council_vote 0x53EB50, propose_treaty 0x544E40, call_off_vendetta 0x54BEC0 are engine addresses, and Thinker's only involvement is patching VALUATION helpers into them (mod_tech_val at 0x53F34B and 0x54547F, mod_wants_to_attack at 0x54C352). A better price for a trade is not a decision about whether to trade.
- base.disband: mod_base_kill (base.cpp:225) is the mechanism, with no deliberate AI caller — as game-surface.md already records.

So base.retool was special for a specific reason worth naming: its 'decision' is not a separate call site at all, it is a penalty folded into production scoring, so the tier arrived as a side effect of Thinker improving base.production. That is the shape to look for elsewhere — a surface whose answer is already implied by a chooser Thinker has improved — and it did not recur among these 13.

======================================================================

IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-16. Thinker 7cc17a8, NeuralAmplifier 0e98fb2.

The finding held up: nothing here needed a deterministic tier built. Three parts landed,
per the epic's rule of one surface / one config flag / one probe:

  na_retool_observe                        default 0, so an unconfigured build is unchanged
  na_observe_base_retool                   the world view (neural.cpp)
  observe-retool <base_id> [chosen_item]   serialiser-only probe

ONE DESIGN CHANGE from what this bead described. The record does NOT sit inside
select_build's retool branch. That branch is where the engine asks the question, but the
ANSWER is what select_build returns, and it returns from six places. A record written at
the question alone carries the inputs to a decision and not the decision — useless on the
one surface whose entire justification is that a working baseline already exists. So
select_build is now a thin wrapper over select_build_inner: production_id_last is read
before the call, check_retool after (same answer either way, nothing in the chooser touches
minerals_accumulated), and native_choice is the two mod_base_making categories compared.
That comparison IS the engine's answer, not an inference about it.

check_retool stays the single definition of when minerals are at risk. na_retool_penalty
exposes it to both the gate and the emitted penalty_applies field, so the two cannot drift
apart into a rule the engine no longer follows.

TWO DEFECTS caught by transcribing the record into test_adapter_contract, both before it
ever ran:

  - the outer item was emitted as `current_item`, colliding with the `current_item`
    na_write_base_state already writes inside base_state. On THIS surface those two disagree
    by construction — the disagreement is the decision — so the record would have carried
    two same-named contradicting fields with no way to tell which one the categories came
    from. Renamed previous_item / previous_item_name.
  - the record had no native_choice at all. See the design change above.

Verified: thinker builds clean, 43 wire checks pass, just check 9/9, 636 orchestrator tests
pass. Each of the three new contract tests was checked to FAIL when the fact it pins is
broken, rather than assumed to.

NOT VERIFIED against a running game — no engine has fired this hook. A retool decision needs
a base mid-build with the chooser wanting a different category, which is far too rare to
catch by playing. That is what the probe is for, and unlike the live path it deliberately
does not gate on the penalty applying, so it can be used to check the wire format on any base.

No captured fixture added: fixtures/captured holds real harvests only (na-oh5, na-ibh), and
fabricating one would defeat the only thing those files are for.

FOLLOW-UP: base.retool stays in OBSERVED and out of APPLIED. It is not covered until a decide
path exists, and there is no reason to build one until the observation has been seen against
a real game.
close_reason: Closed

title: Order-scoped board effects: a guard cannot deny a move it cannot describe
description:
The yupana board guard can now SEE bases (thinker na_board_state publishes them) but still cannot deny an order that would break a board policy, because Action.effects is dict[str, float] keyed on the METRICS vocabulary and lands on the synthetic faction node (yupana.py FACTION_NODE).

So 'disbanding this unit empties an exposed base's garrison' is inexpressible: the order carries no node-scoped effect, yupana's overlay sees the board unchanged, and the policy can only fire pre_existing — which correctly WARNS rather than strips, because the order did not cause the condition.

Measured 2026-08-16: with an exposed base at garrison_count 0 the guard returns warn with 'already true before these orders (?b=base:1, ?d=8)'. Useful — the brain is told — but it is not enforcement.

NOT urgent, and that is the point of filing rather than building it: every surface whose orders would move a base's garrison is unit-scope and in surfaces.NO_AI_PATH, so the brain cannot decide one today. This becomes real the moment a unit-scope surface is instrumented (na-yd4), and doing it before then would be a contract change serving nothing.

Sketch: an optional Action.board_effects carrying yupana OrderEffect shapes ({op,id,key,value}), passed through by yupana.proposed() alongside the metric deltas it already derives. The adapter states them; the model never does — an order's consequences are the engine's statement about itself, and taking them from the answer would let a brain describe its move as harmless and be believed.

Acceptance: an order that would empty an exposed base's garrison is DENIED with that order id stripped, not merely warned about.
close_reason:
Done, and the acceptance criterion is met verbatim: an order that would empty an exposed base's garrison is DENIED with that order id stripped, not merely warned about. Verified against a live yupana.

Action.board_effects (contract.py) carries yupana OrderEffect shapes — [{"op":"set_attr","id":"base:1","key":"garrison_count","value":0}] — saying what an action does to a NAMED ENTITY rather than to a faction-level measurement. yupana.proposed() forwards them alongside the metric deltas it already derived.

Measured before/after on the same policy and board: an order emptying base:1 (defend_range 8, garrison 1 -> 0) now returns verdict=deny, stripped=('disband:u7',) with the policy's own claim; the alternative returns allow. Previously the same situation could only produce 'already true before these orders' — a pre_existing finding, correctly warning and never enforcing, because no order could express changing the board.

THE OTHER HALF IS TESTED AND MATTERS AS MUCH: a base that was ALREADY empty still only warns. An order must not be denied for a condition it did not cause, however expressible that condition has become. Both directions have a live test.

Three design points held from the bead:
- ADAPTER-STATED, NEVER MODEL-STATED. An order's consequences are the engine's claim about itself; taking them from the answer would let a brain describe its own move as harmless and be believed.
- Attribute names are namespaced on the way out. The adapter states plain `garrison_count` because the contract must not carry a graph's vocabulary; an effect forwarded unprefixed would set an attribute no selector can see — silently, and looking exactly like a policy that passed.
- An op yupana does not know is DROPPED rather than forwarded. Forwarding it is refused at the far end and takes the whole guard call down, so one adapter typo would cost the board check on every decision instead of the one effect it got wrong. A non-object entry is refused earlier still, by the contract type, where the adapter can see the error.

I had earlier argued this was premature because every surface whose orders move a garrison is unit-scope and in NO_AI_PATH. That was an argument about when it becomes USEFUL, not about whether it could be built or verified — both of which it can, with a synthetic world view. The plumbing is now in place and correct for the day na-yd4 instruments such a surface.

6 tests: 4 offline on the mapping, 2 live on the deny/warn split.

title: Adapter: publish board fields so the yupana board policies can fire
description:
The yupana board guard is wired (yupana.py, NA_YUPANA_URL) and evaluating. Two of the three starter policies in policies/board.example.json are inert because WorldView.bases carries none of the attributes they select on: smac:isBorderBase, smac:garrisonCount, smac:underThreat, and a faction-level smac:expanding.

Not silent — yupana reports each as 'vacuous' on every decision, so the gap is on the record rather than passing as a clean board. That is the point of shipping them inert, and it is also the acceptance signal here.

Acceptance: the Thinker adapter publishes those fields into WorldView.bases (and the expansion flag into metrics); garrison-border-bases and hold-expansion-under-threat stop appearing under 'policy matched nothing' and start producing real findings. No orchestrator change should be needed — the guard reads whatever the adapter publishes, prefixed smac:.

Note the byte-for-byte vocabulary rule: yupana does no prefix expansion, and yupana.py prefixes every ingested key with smac:. An adapter field named isBorderBase becomes smac:isBorderBase, which is what the policy must name.
notes:
PARTLY DONE 2026-08-16 — the adapter half landed.

scbrown/thinker, branch claude/neural-amplifier-progress-sg3ojv, commit 0028451: na_write_bases publishes this faction's own bases in every world view behind na_board_state (default 0). Hung off na_write_head rather than the thirteen na_write_metrics call sites so every decision carries it by construction. Own bases only — another faction's would be an information cheat of the same kind the diplomacy fog gate stops.

Deliberately the ENGINE'S OWN INTEGERS, not the derived booleans this bead originally asked for. isBorderBase would put a threshold inside the DLL where nobody can change it without a cross-compiler, and it answers a judgement question the adapter has no business answering. So defend_range / garrison_count / defend_goal go out as facts and policies/board.example.json owns the threshold (< 12, which is what Thinker's own build code treats as 'wants perimeter defence').

Two properties of defend_range that a policy MUST NOT misread, documented in neural.cpp, docs/thinker.ini and policies/README.md: it is NOT tiles (plan.cpp weights map_range by region and war state, halves, caps at 50 — lower means more exposed, and the same neighbour scores 8 at war and 32 at peace), and it refreshes once per faction turn while world views are emitted at decision time.

NA side: test_yupana.py pins the adapter's field names and asserts every attribute the starter policies select on is one the adapter actually publishes — so a rename on either side fails CI rather than showing up as a 'vacuous' note on every decision of a real game.

STILL OPEN, which is why this stays open: the base policies can only WARN. Action.effects is keyed on the metrics vocabulary and lands on the faction node, so 'this order empties that base's garrison' is inexpressible, yupana's overlay sees the board unchanged, and the finding returns pre_existing. Tracked as na-n72, deliberately unbuilt — every surface whose orders would move a garrison is unit-scope and in NO_AI_PATH.

NOT VERIFIED IN A RUNNING GAME. The serializer needs a real SMAC install; the fork's own wire tests (38 checks, green) cover only the HTTP client. What is verified is the cross-repo contract: the exact payload na_write_bases emits, run through WorldView -> yupana.entities -> yupana_guard against a live yupana, fires the garrison policy on an exposed empty base.
UNBLOCKED AND DONE 2026-08-16.

The one reason this bead stayed open was that the base policies could only WARN:
Action.effects is keyed on the metrics vocabulary and lands on the faction node, so "this
order empties that base's garrison" was inexpressible and every finding came back
pre_existing. That is na-n72, and na-n72 is closed. Action.board_effects now carries
yupana OrderEffect shapes naming a specific entity, yupana.proposed() forwards them, and
test_an_order_that_empties_an_exposed_base_is_denied_not_merely_warned shows verdict=deny
with the offending order id stripped — against a live yupana, not a mock. Its counterpart
test_a_base_already_empty_still_only_warns holds the other direction, which matters just as
much: an order must not be denied for a condition it did not cause.

ACCEPTANCE, restated because the bead's original wording is stale. It asked for
smac:isBorderBase / smac:underThreat / smac:expanding and named two policies that no longer
exist. The adapter deliberately publishes the ENGINE'S OWN INTEGERS instead — defend_range,
garrison_count, defend_goal — and policies/board.example.json owns the thresholds. Putting
isBorderBase in the DLL would bury a judgement call where nobody can change it without a
cross-compiler. The starter policies are now reserves-stay-solvent,
garrison-exposed-bases and meet-the-defence-goal-when-close, and none of them is vacuous:
test_the_starter_policies_select_on_fields_the_adapter_publishes asserts every attribute
they select on is one na_write_bases actually emits, so a rename on either side fails CI
instead of showing up as a 'policy matched nothing' note on every decision of a real game.

STILL NOT VERIFIED IN A RUNNING GAME, and this is the honest limit. The serializer needs a
real SMAC install. What IS verified end to end is the cross-repo contract: the exact payload
na_write_bases emits, run through WorldView -> yupana.entities -> yupana_guard against a
live yupana, firing the garrison policy on an exposed empty base. Closing on that basis
rather than leaving it open on a condition no amount of code can satisfy here; a live-game
check belongs with the other play-blocked beads.

NOT IN SCOPE and not a gap: no instrumented surface emits board_effects yet, because every
surface whose orders would move a garrison is unit-scope and in NO_AI_PATH. The plumbing is
correct and waiting for na-yd4.
close_reason: Closed

title: [BUG] regenerating prompts destroys the manifest records that exist to outlive regeneration
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-06 while regenerating na-htm's prompts for na-5to. Found by reading the diff of
a routine `just eval prompts`, not by looking for it.

`write_prompts` (evals/harness.py) rebuilt the manifest from scratch and carried forward exactly
ONE key from the existing file, by name:

    manifest["answered_by"] = existing.get("answered_by", "unrecorded")

Every other human-authored key was silently destroyed. Two casualties, and both exist
specifically to outlive a regeneration:

1. **`grounding_pinned`** (top level) — where the pin came from, when it was harvested, why it
   was re-pinned, and the refresh command. Destroyed on na-htm in this session; restored.

2. **each arm's `drift_reviewed`** — worse, because `check_prompts`' own docstring is what tells
   people to record it there, at length, calling its pinned-both-hashes shape "the whole point"
   and explaining that it is the only thing letting the staleness check go green AND be able to
   go red again. `write_prompts` rebuilt `manifest["arms"][name]` wholesale, so it went too.
   Live instances at risk when found: 6 (na-373 all, na-61c2 x3, na-vbe x2), each carrying a
   multi-sentence adjudication by sattler dated 2026-08-03.

So the writer destroyed the record the reader documents. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the
regenerated manifest looks entirely well-formed — the loss is only visible in a git diff, and
only if someone reads it.

## Fix (applied, same commit as na-5to's fix)

Invert the rule: name what the CODE owns and preserve everything else.

    _DERIVED_TOP = frozenset({"note", "arms"})
    _DERIVED_ARM = frozenset({"prompt_sha256", "facts_offered", "options"})

An allowlist is the wrong shape here and is precisely why it broke — it must be extended every
time somebody records something new, and forgetting is silent. Under the inverted rule a key
nobody anticipated survives by default.

VERIFIED: re-ran `just eval prompts na-htm` after the fix — `grounding_pinned` survives and the
only manifest lines that move are the three `ranked` prompt hashes that na-5to genuinely changes.
`just eval check` prints all 6 `drift_reviewed` adjudications intact.

## Not fixed here — a separate question worth a decision

`prompts` still overwrites `prompt_sha256` itself, which silently re-baselines staleness for any
eval that HAS committed answers. `check_prompts`' docstring names that exact move as the tempting
wrong one: "re-hashing the manifest so the check goes quiet erases the only signal that the
answers are old". Today nothing stops `just eval prompts <id>` from doing it to a paid run.

Not changed unilaterally because it is a workflow-semantics call, not a bug fix: regenerating
prompts legitimately means "these are new inputs". The options are (a) refuse to regenerate an
arm that has committed answers without an explicit flag, (b) warn loudly and name the arms, or
(c) leave it and rely on review. Recommend (a) — it matches how the rest of this directory
treats committed evidence — but it should be someone's decision, not a side effect of this bug.
close_reason: Fix was already applied in the tree — evals/harness.py carries _DERIVED_TOP/_DERIVED_ARM and the inverted preserve-by-default rule the bead specifies (harness.py:156-157, 197-203). Verified by inspection this session; nothing left to do. The follow-up question the bead deliberately left open — whether 'just eval prompts' should refuse to re-baseline prompt_sha256 for an arm with committed answers — is filed separately below.

title: Drop the stale VALUES/FILTER IN workaround in the Quipu datalink
description:
datalinks/quipu.py:89 builds a manual `?v = "a" || ?v = "b"` disjunction with the comment "Quipu rejects both VALUES and FILTER IN." That comment is stale — both features landed in Quipu:

- VALUES: `GraphPattern::Values` is evaluated in src/sparql/pattern.rs:65 (quipu #51), joining through the ordinary Join/LeftJoin arms.
- IN / NOT IN: `Expression::In` is evaluated in src/sparql/filter.rs:35; NOT IN parses as `Not(In(..))`.

Cost of keeping it: _disjunction() emits one comparison per label per variable, so the FILTER grows linearly with the turn's action space — the exact prompt-bounded path build_query() is trying to keep tight. VALUES is also the semantically correct construct: it is an inline relation that joins, so the engine can use it to seed the BGP rather than scanning and filtering afterwards.

Fix: replace the two _disjunction() calls in build_query() with a VALUES block binding ?label and ?eng, delete _disjunction() and its stale comment, and confirm against the pinned Quipu rev before merging (verify, do not assume — the original comment was presumably true when written).

Watch for: escape() is currently applied inside _disjunction; the VALUES rewrite still needs literal escaping. test_datalinks.py covers build_query output, so update the expected SPARQL there.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
Adjudicated and pushed as bcf1bd8. `just eval check` exits 0 again, and can still go red.

## RE-RAN vs RE-REASONED — asked for explicitly, so stated first

**I re-ran NOTHING against a model. Zero of the three.** No arm was re-answered; no tokens were
spent. Every manifest record carries `re_run: false` so a future reader cannot assume otherwise.

What I DID measure (free, re-derivable):

  - the exact prompt diff, per cell
  - that the diff is byte-identical across arms within each eval
  - that `turns_to_completion` appears in no arm's world-view payload and in none of the
    committed prompts
  - which retriever each eval uses, and whether its limit bites

What I REASONED from those measurements: that an addition which is identical on both sides of a
between-arm comparison cannot move that comparison. That is the load-bearing step and it is
reasoning, not measurement. It could be wrong if the added text interacted with the arms
asymmetrically — which is why the record pins the hashes rather than erasing them.

## YOUR COMPOUNDING HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED — by mechanism, not by assurance

It was the right thing to ask and it is testable for free. All three older evals use
`DatalinksRetriever`, not `QuipuRetriever`. na-dhs was a QuipuRetriever-only defect:

    retriever          DatalinksRetriever
    limit              12
    options in fixture 8
    facts retrieved    8
    limit bites?       False        <- so no truncation, before or after
    has a query step?  False        <- the na-dhs defect was in the SPARQL candidate list

Three independent reasons it cannot compound: wrong class; DatalinksRetriever applies its limit
to RESULTS (append-then-break), never to candidates, so the bug's shape cannot exist there; and
with 8 options against a limit of 12 it never fires anyway.

So "stale" does not understate it by that route. The answers are outdated, not wrong.

## What actually moved — three lines, identical in all seven cells

    + one metric-VOCABULARY line for `turns_to_completion`
    + "decision_deadline_ms": null
    + "run_id": null

COMMON-MODE: 1 distinct diff per eval across 2, 3 and 2 arms. INERT: `turns_to_completion`
describes a metric these fixtures do not carry — 0 occurrences in every committed prompt and in
every regenerated payload.

## Remedy: a PINNED adjudication, which is not option (b)

I proposed three options on this bead. (a) re-answer, (b) re-hash, (c) mark and leave it red.
I did none of them, because there is a better one and (b) vs (c) is a false choice.

`drift_reviewed` in the manifest stores BOTH hashes — the one the answers were measured against
and the one adjudicated. `prompt_sha256` is never overwritten. So:

  - `check` prints `ok (drift reviewed 2026-08-03 by sattler) — <reason>` for exactly that pair;
  - ANY further change makes a third hash, matches no review, and goes STALE again — naming the
    review that failed to cover it, so a stale adjudication cannot be read as a current one.

Why not (b): re-hashing erases the only signal that the answers are old, and it is most tempting
precisely when the drift looks harmless. Why not (c): a check that stays red forever gets
ignored — which is how these seven cells went unnoticed in the first place. A pinned
adjudication is the only version that can go green AND go red again.

## Controlled BOTH ways, because a check that could only go green would be the bug

    green: just eval check                                  -> exit 0
    red:   perturb _SYSTEM after the review, re-check       -> 7/7 STALE, one line each,
                                                               each naming the stale review

## Not closed by this, deliberately

na-373's finding stays WITHDRAWN and ranking stays `unmeasured` — that was never about prompt
drift. And na-5to still stands: `information_value` is flat on real grounding, which is a defect
in the RULE, not in the prompt these answers were measured against.

title: QuipuRetriever truncates to 12 LABELS before querying, so a 48-option decision grounds 7 options
description:
Found while building na-htm's multi-decision eval (commit d671e1a).

quipu.py retrieve(): `labels = list(dict.fromkeys(candidates))[: self.limit]` — the limit is
applied to the CANDIDATE LABELS before the SPARQL query, not to the facts that come back.

MEASURED, not inferred, against the committed capture base_production_turn135.json
(University, turn 135, 48 build options) with quipu-server on .quipu/na.db:

    48 options in the action space
    12 labels queried (the first 12 in action-space order)
     7 facts returned

So 41 of 48 options reach the model with no grounding at all, and WHICH 41 is decided by
action-space order rather than by anything about the decision.

Why this matters beyond the count: na-373's stated mechanism for how truncation hurts is that
grounding is roughly one fact per option, so dropping a fact removes the argument for a
PARTICULAR option, and an unexplained option loses. If that mechanism is real, it is already
operating on 41 of 48 options before any eval arm acts — silently, and invisibly in the record,
which shows which facts were offered but never which options were left unargued.

Two candidate fixes, and they are not equivalent:
  (a) apply the limit to RESULTS rather than to candidate labels — every option gets asked
      about, and the cut falls on what the store actually knows;
  (b) raise the limit for large action spaces, which trades prompt budget for coverage.

(a) is the one that changes which options are represented; (b) only changes how many. Neither
is obviously right and this needs the budget discipline in docs/quipu-integration.md read
alongside it — filing rather than fixing.

Does not invalidate na-htm: citations there are scored against the ranking of what was
actually offered.
close_reason:
Fixed and pushed as d73081c. Falsifiable by re-measurement against the live store: base.production t135 went 7 -> 20 grounded options, and the 13 recovered facts are all facilities (the category the cap systematically ate, since action spaces list units first). The cap bought no latency — 12, 24 and 48 labels all returned in ~1151 ms, the query time being flat in the disjunction size.

Fix: the query asks about every option; query_labels (64) guards query SHAPE only; limit applies to RESULTS and defaults off, with token_budget as the real bound since it bounds prompt size and records what it sheds. Grounding gains shed/unmatched (opposite remedies — 28 of those 48 options are simply absent from the graph, previously indistinguishable from our truncation), and knowledge.summarise now assembles retrieval advisories, which retrieval had no channel for at all.

528 passed. The test that asserted the defect was the only one in the file with no docstring; replaced with the inverse contract plus two for the shed/unmatched split.

FOUND WHILE VERIFYING THIS, filed as na-5to (P1): information_value is FLAT on real grounding — 2 distinct scores over 40 facts — because it splits the option name on an em dash only na-373's fixture emits. That blocks the na-uwp paid run harder than this did, and na-htm's dominance gate would not have caught it.

title: Make directive-issuing reachable: the model never uses it, even when invited (na-j2w)
description:
na-j2w measured it: ZERO directives issued across twenty runs of faction.tech, including the ten where the system prompt explicitly invited them. The path works — na-43h proved it live, issue on faction.tech, shown on a later base.production — but that used a scripted driver that issued deliberately.

So the gap is not the mechanism. Nothing makes issuing attractive at the moment of decision: the model is asked to pick a technology, and setting faction policy is optional extra work with no visible payoff inside that turn.

CHEAPEST THING TO TRY FIRST, and there is precedent: Orders.cited was explained in the system prompt and came back empty on every run until the explanation moved into the SCHEMA, where the model reads it. Orders.directives already carries a field description for the same reason. Check whether it actually says WHEN to issue rather than what a directive is — 'expected only where the world view shows a long horizon' is a note to a reader, not an instruction to a model choosing a tech.

Second: the world view may simply not show a horizon worth planning over. faction.tech fires every 5-10 turns but its world view is one turn deep.

This blocks any rerun of na-j2w. Until an arm issues, there is no treatment to measure and a larger sample only buys a more confident zero.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
## STEP ONE ANSWERED, and the answer is worse than the bead guessed (ellie, measured 2026-08-03)

The bead names the cheapest first check: "Check whether [the field description] actually says WHEN
to issue rather than what a directive is". Done. There are TWO directive field descriptions, and
**the model is shown the wrong one.**

### The model-facing schema says nine words, and they are a SUPPRESSOR

`response.py` states its own purpose in its first line:

    "The shapes we ask a model to fill in, as distinct from the shape we pass around."

It exists because the wire contract is `extra="allow"` (unbounded grammar) and too large for
structured output. `brain.py` is its only importer — this IS the structured-output path.

    response.py:113   directives: list[DirectiveOut] = Field(
                          description="Standing intent for FUTURE decisions. Empty unless setting direction."

That is the entire instruction the model receives. It contains NO "when". Its one actionable
clause — "Empty unless setting direction" — points at empty.

### All of the WHEN guidance lives in the schema the model never sees

    contract.py:450   description=(
        "Standing strategic intent to place on FUTURE decisions, WHEN THIS DECISION COMMITS TO A
         PLAN THAT LATER TURNS MUST FOLLOW TO BE WORTH ANYTHING. Leave empty unless you are
         genuinely setting direction. `metric` must be one of the metric names listed in the system
         prompt — a directive naming anything else is discarded, because it could never be checked.
         Use at_least/at_most with a `target` for an absolute bound, or increase/decrease/hold to be
         measured against the value at issue time. Set `horizon_turn` to ..."

~700 characters, including the only sentence that answers "when", the metric constraint, the
bound semantics, and horizon_turn. `contract.py` is the wire contract — "the shape we pass
around". The model never reads it.

### This is the Orders.cited precedent EXACTLY, one layer over

The bead cites it: `cited` was explained in the system prompt, came back empty every run, and only
worked once the explanation moved into the schema the model reads. `directives` was given a field
description for that same reason — but it was added to the WRONG SCHEMA. The fix that worked for
`cited` was applied here in form and missed in substance.

So the twenty-run zero is not surprising and does not need a larger sample to confirm. A model
reading "Empty unless setting direction", with no statement of when a directive pays off and no
in-turn payoff, will return empty essentially every time. The measurement was correct; the arm
was never actually installed.

### CONCRETE FIX DIRECTION for whoever takes this

Move the WHEN clause — and only that — into `response.py`'s directives description. Specifically
the "when this decision commits to a plan that later turns must follow to be worth anything" half,
which is the trigger condition, NOT the metric/bound/horizon mechanics (those are validation
concerns and belong where they are).

Mind the constraint response.py's own docstring flags: **"Size is a hard limit, not a soft cost.
Adding nested Directive objects to Orders took ..."** — so this must be a tight rewrite, not a
paste of the 700-char version. Suggested shape, ~25 words instead of 9:

    "Standing intent for FUTURE decisions. Issue one when THIS choice commits to a plan later
     turns must follow to be worth anything; otherwise leave empty."

That keeps the suppressor (so it does not become noise) but gives it a positive trigger to weigh
against, which the current text lacks entirely.

### Second hypothesis in the bead — NOT investigated

"the world view may simply not show a horizon worth planning over ... faction.tech fires every
5-10 turns but its world view is one turn deep." Untouched. If the schema fix alone does not move
the count off zero, that is the next thing, and it is a bigger change.

### STATUS: handing back, not stalling

Not taking this further in this session for a stated reason, not a vague one: `st tend --status`
reports `governor seven_day usage 78% · 75% tier · dispatch only P0 and above; only support crew
runs`. This is P2. Starting a build-and-eval cycle against that governor is the wrong call, and
the remaining work (edit schema, re-run the na-j2w eval arm, measure) needs a clean session
anyway.

Unassigning so it returns to the pool ready to go. It is NOT blocked and should NOT be deferred —
step one is done and the fix is specified above; someone can pick this up and go straight to the
edit.

change it fired on — and the failure that file exists to prevent is precisely the silent one: a
too-large schema makes the API reject every request, every decision degrades to the native answer,
and the stability harness reports a clean 1.00 over ten identical fallbacks.

headroom went from 51 b to 28 b, so the next description added here needs a measurement, not a
guess.

  - the directives description must not be PURELY a suppressor — it has to state when to issue,
    not only when not to. Pinned because this exact bug has now recurred once in this file, by
    this route (`cited` first, `directives` second).

526 tests pass, mypy clean (35 files), ruff clean.

honest state is "the instruction the model reads now contains a trigger", not "the model issues
directives". Confirming that is a rerun of the na-j2w eval, which this bead was blocking — a zero

faction.tech fires every 5-10 turns but its world view is one turn deep, so there may be no
horizon visible worth planning over. That is a bigger change than a description.

title: Does asking a model to decide AND set direction make it do either worse? (na-43h item b)
description:
Split out of na-43h, whose acceptance (item a) is met and closed. This is the measurement half and it costs model spend.

Run faction.tech through scripts/decision_stability.py with --brain claude-code, issue_directives ON and OFF, and compare stability and choice.

The ablation is VERIFIED SOUND, which is what makes the comparison trustworthy: _strip_issuing removes 2944 chars of the real system prompt, cuts '## Issuing directives' and KEEPS '## Standing directives'. An ablation that cut both would confound 'not allowed to issue' with 'cannot see directives at all' and would look like a clean answer to a question it never asked.

Score the choice distribution as well as stability — a model that becomes more consistent while choosing worse is not an improvement, and stability alone cannot tell those apart.

title: Faction aggregates read 0 on base.production for factions whose turn is not being processed — a false zero in the setback denominator
description:
Found while running the na-s4e build A/B (evals/runs/na-s4e). NOT caused by that fix — both
build arms agree, so it predates thinker 0722b7b.

On the base.production surface, factions whose turn is not being processed report faction-scope
aggregates as ZERO while other fields on the same record are populated:

    fid=2 Hive        base.production  energy_income 0  labs_output 0   energy_reserves 707  base_count 49
    fid=3 University  base.production  energy_income 0  labs_output 0   energy_reserves 547  base_count 55

A 49-base faction does not have zero gross energy and zero labs output. The same factions report
sane values on other surfaces at the same turn:

    fid=2 Hive        faction.tech     energy_income  6  labs_output  25
    fid=3 University  faction.tech     energy_income 127 labs_output 396
    fid=3 University  faction.se       energy_income 353 labs_output 610

So the aggregates (Faction.energy_surplus_total, turn_commerce_income, facility_maint_total,
labs_total) are evidently not refreshed at the base.production observation point for a faction
whose turn is not currently being processed — while energy_credits and base_count, which are not
per-turn recomputed aggregates, stay correct.

WHY THIS MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A CURIOSITY. metrics.energy_income is the denominator of
setback_turns (directives.py RATE_OF -> _setback). A directive evaluated against one of these
world views divides by zero, or reads a zero as a real measurement. "Not computed yet" and
"genuinely zero" are the same two characters in the record, and a faction whose net income really
IS zero is a state the vocabulary is supposed to be able to represent — that is precisely what
na-s4e made representable.

This is the failure shape the project keeps meeting: a value that reports without having checked,
read as though it had checked. It is worse here than a missing field, because a missing field is
visibly missing and a zero looks like an answer.

SHAPE OF A FIX — decision needed, which is why this is a bead and not a patch:
  (a) omit the metrics block entirely when the aggregates are known stale, so the orchestrator
      sees a missing field rather than a false zero (directives already handle UNMEASURABLE, and
      _setback already omits rather than invents when the rate is absent);
  (b) emit the faction's aggregates only on surfaces where its turn IS being processed;
  (c) stamp the record with a freshness flag and let the orchestrator decide.

(a) is my recommendation — it uses the path that already exists for "cannot measure this", and it
makes the ambiguity unrepresentable rather than documented. Whoever owns the adapter's observation
path should pick.

Reproduce: evals/runs/na-s4e/{net,gross}.metrics.jsonl, rows with surface_id base.production and
faction_id 2 or 3.

title: metrics.energy_income reports gross base energy, not income — setback_turns is systematically optimistic
description:
metrics.energy_income reports GROSS base energy, not income: it omits facility maintenance and
commerce, so every setback_turns computed from it is systematically optimistic.

neural.cpp:404   na_buf_printf(w, ",\"energy_income\":%d", plr.energy_surplus_total);

energy_surplus_total is not net income:
  base.cpp:2307    per-base contribution is clamp(base->energy_surplus, 0, 99999) - a base in
                   energy deficit contributes 0, not a negative, so it is not even a true sum.
  game.cpp:1824-8  under RFLAG_INTEREST with rule_interest == 0, +1 per base is folded in here.
  game.cpp:1833    f->unk_17 = f->energy_surplus_total + f->turn_commerce_income
                               - f->facility_maint_total;
                   The engine computes true net SEPARATELY. So energy_surplus_total excludes
                   commerce and does not subtract maintenance.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE NAME. The value is the denominator of the only piece of hard
arithmetic the directive block shows a model:

  metrics.energy_income  ->  RATE_OF["energy_reserves"]  (directives.py:34)
                         ->  _setback: turns = abs(delta)/abs(rate)  (directives.py:430)
                         ->  setback_turns

A faction whose facility maintenance nearly consumes its gross energy is told that hurrying costs
a couple of turns of progress when the real recovery is far longer - or never, if net income is
<= 0, a case the current value cannot even represent because it is always >= 0.

_setback's docstring already names this failure mode: "A setback figure with an invented
denominator is worse than no figure, because it looks like the one piece of hard arithmetic in
the block." The denominator is not invented here, it is mislabelled, which is the same failure
with better paperwork. na_write_metrics' own docstring says "nothing here is estimated" - true of
the arithmetic, not of the name.

PROPOSED FIX - the engine's own expression, so it stays arithmetic rather than becoming an
estimate:

  na_buf_printf(w, ",\"energy_income\":%d",
      plr.energy_surplus_total + plr.turn_commerce_income - plr.facility_maint_total);

DECISION NEEDED, which is why this is a bead and not a patch: this changes the MEANING of a name
in the shared metrics vocabulary that directive evaluation divides by. The alternatives are (a)
change the value as above, (b) keep the value and rename the metric to something honest like
energy_gross, or (c) emit both. (a) is my recommendation - "income" is the name a directive
author will reach for, so the name should be right and the value should follow it. Whoever owns
metrics.py should pick.

NOT verified at runtime: no SMAC fixture on this host, so this is read from source across the
full chain rather than observed in a game. Found while working na-b4v, which asked for exactly
this metric's semantics to be checked rather than assumed.

title: Comms surfaces must issue directives - a diplomacy answer is a promise about later turns
description:
A diplomacy answer is a PROMISE about future turns, so the comms surface must issue a directive or the answer is a lie the game never notices.

Live case, turn 38 (2138), Peacekeepers vs Lord's Believers, status TREATY. Miriam:

  "Perhaps your troops failed to notice my large boundary markers when they illegally
   intruded into my territory. Would you kindly comply with our Treaty of Friendship by
   removing your forces at once?"

  1. "Withdraw troops to nearest base."
  2. "Only if you likewise withdraw from my territory!"
  3. "I have decided to make certain 'adjustments' to our borders, Miriam."

Option 1 commits us to move units OFF Believer tiles. Nothing in the current design carries that commitment past the dialog: the answer is applied to the diplomacy state and the conclusion dies with the response, which is the exact failure Directive was built for (contract.py, Directive docstring). The unit-movement decisions on later turns would have no idea a promise was made, so we would answer "yes, at once", leave the troops where they are, and take the treaty-break consequences without ever having decided to.

Option 2 is worse in the same way - it is a CONDITIONAL promise, so it also needs the condition tracked.

BLOCKED TWICE, both concrete:

1. METRIC VOCABULARY CANNOT EXPRESS IT (na-c17). Directive.metric must name something in
   metrics.py or the directive is rejected at issue time by design. The vocabulary is
   faction-level economics - energy_reserves, energy_income, labs_output, base_count, pop_total,
   military_units. There is no metric for "own units standing on another faction's territory",
   so the directive that this decision most obviously needs cannot be written at all. na-c17
   already says most directives cannot be expressed; this is a concrete, motivating instance of
   it rather than a new problem.

   The metric this case wants is roughly `units_in_foreign_territory` (count, lower is better,
   per-faction), which is also the metric that makes the promise CHECKABLE next turn - the whole
   point of the type. That is cheap for the adapter to compute: it already sweeps bases for
   drone_total, and a sweep over Vehs testing tile ownership is the same shape.

2. NOTHING WOULD RECEIVE IT. Even with the metric, directives reach a decision through
   relevant() - hop 0 matches an action whose `effects` touch the metric, or an entity the
   decision is about. There is no unit-movement LLM surface, and unit moves do not declare
   `effects`. So the directive would be in force, unmeasurable, and shown to nobody, which reads
   in the PlanBlock as a plan being served (unmeasurable, not unsatisfied) when it is inert.

ALSO BLOCKING THE SURFACE ITSELF: diplo.tribute is `demand_withdrawal` (engine.cpp:755), marked
in docs/game-surface.md as a raw engine pointer with no Thinker override - which is why it is one
of the ❌ rows. Intercepting it needs the central mod_popp wrapper (na-4lr). Until then the dialog
can only be driven through the na-input channel by clicking, which works but has no world view,
no action space and no decision record.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS FOR: the design rule, and the order of work. The rule is that any surface whose
answer is a commitment about later turns MUST issue a directive as part of its response, and the
acceptance for such a surface is not "it answered" but "a later turn acted on the answer".
diplo.tribute is the clearest instance because the promise is explicit and immediate, but
diplo.treaty_offer, diplo.surrender and the pact surfaces are all the same shape.

Suggested order: na-c17 (metric) -> a units/territory metric in the adapter -> na-4lr (dialog
interception) -> this surface. Doing the surface first produces a brain that makes promises
nothing can keep, which is worse than not having the surface.

Noted while trying to run this exact conversation through the brain: NA_BRAIN is "scripted" in
na.toml and there is no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment, so no real decision could be made
for it in that session either.
notes:
PROGRESS 2026-08-16 — blocker 1 of 3 is lifted. The other two stand.

BLOCKER 1 (metric vocabulary) DONE. units_in_foreign_territory now exists on both sides:
- scbrown/thinker @ 362052c, na_write_metrics — a sweep over Vehs, the same shape as the drone sweep over Bases, counting this faction's units whose tile whose_territory() attributes to somebody else.
- metrics.py — faction scope, units, lower is better, not a pool.
- test_metrics_vocabulary.py — the seam set updated, plus two tests that write the actual Miriam promise as a Directive and evaluate it: at_most 0 reads current=3 satisfied=False with troops on her land, and current=0 satisfied=True once they are out.

Two properties chosen deliberately, both worth keeping if this is ever reimplemented:
- FOG-RESPECTING BY CONSTRUCTION. whose_territory returns -1 for an owner we have no commlink with, so land belonging to a faction we have never met does not count. We cannot have promised anything to a faction we have not met, and counting it would leak that faction's existence into a number the brain reads.
- POSITION, NOT INTENT. A unit already marching home still counts until it is out. That is what lets the number fall as the promise is KEPT rather than the moment it is made — a metric that read orders would go satisfied instantly and measure nothing.

title: Multi-decision retrieval-ranking eval — one world view cannot measure a ranking rule
description:
na-373's refutation was withdrawn on re-measurement (see evals/runs/na-373/NOTES.md) and its
reversal is no more trustworthy. Both numbers reduce to a single fact's rank: 19 of 27 baseline
citations are fac:network-node, so 'citations in the top k' is really 'did network-node make the
cut'. The choice-stability half has the same defect from the other side — base.production at
turn 35 is 19/20 for one option, so an arm can only move it down, and a rule that keeps the
winner's fact looks harmless whatever else it does.

What would actually decide it:

- several world views, not one. Different surfaces (base.production, base.hurry, faction.tech)
  and different turns, so no single fact dominates the citation pool.
- contested decisions, chosen the way na-61c2 chooses its history arm — a near-unanimous world
  view cannot show a ranking doing damage OR doing good.
- score on aggregate citation rank across decisions (mean reciprocal rank or fraction-in-top-k
  pooled over all facts), not on one decision's choice flip.

Until that exists, ranking stays out of the retriever, and the reason recorded is 'unmeasured',
not 'refuted'.

`orchestrator/tests/fixtures/captured/`. No capture run was needed and none was done.

**Aggregate citation rank, not a choice flip.** Each citation contributes its rank inside its
own decision's ranking; MRR and fraction-in-top-4 pool those. Nulls computed PER DECISION
(they carry 5-8 facts, so one shared chance baseline would be wrong for all four) and analytic,
not simulated — no verdict has a random number in its denominator.

**A dominance gate, which is the reason the file exists.** `score` reports the largest share
held by any one fact and any one decision, and REFUSES to print a headline past 0.50. Fed
na-373's own shape it refuses, and that case is a committed control. na-373 could not detect its
own defect; this can.

**Three states, never two.** `NOT RUN` (no answers) / `ANSWERED, BUT NOTHING CITED` / a verdict.
Given a ~1-in-3 citation rate, a scorer that renders the first two as "no effect found" would
publish a dead measurement as a null result.

## What is verified, free, today

`just eval selftest na-htm` — no model, no server, no run. Both nulls and Wilson checked against
hand arithmetic, plus FOUR end-to-end cases where the answer is known before the scorer sees it:

    perfect   every citation at rank 0        -> 1.00, higher than chance, no refusal
    na-373    one fact of one decision x20    -> REFUSING THE HEADLINE, no verdict
    inverted  every citation last             -> anti-predictive, 0.00, no refusal
    uncited   answers present, nothing cited  -> ANSWERED BUT NOTHING CITED, no verdict

All pass. `just eval harvest na-htm`: all 4 decisions match the live retriever. Full suite 526
passed. `just eval check na-htm`: all 8 cells ok — and I control-tested that: perturbing
`_SYSTEM` by one line trips all 8, so the pass is real, not vacuous.

## Two findings from building it

**1. `just eval check` exits 1 — all three OLDER evals are STALE.** na-373 (both arms), na-61c2
(all three) and na-vbe (both) were measured against a system prompt that has since gained
`turns_to_completion` and a contract that gained `decision_deadline_ms`/`run_id`. Pre-existing,
not introduced here. It means na-373's numbers are not evidence about what ships today either —
a third independent reason its result is unmeasured rather than refuted.

**2. The 48-option decision grounds 7 of its options.** `QuipuRetriever` truncates to
`limit=12` LABELS BEFORE QUERYING (`quipu.py`: `labels = [...][: self.limit]`), so on
base.production t135 only the first 12 of 48 options are asked about and 7 resolve. The `all`
arm there is already a heavy truncation of the action space and `ranked` truncates a truncation.
It does not invalidate the rank measurement — citations are scored against the ranking of what
was actually offered — but "every fact the action space pulls" is not what happens on a large
action space. Worth its own bead; not filed yet.

Also corrected three places asserting na-373's withdrawn result as fact: its module docstring,
`information_value`'s (the truncation mechanism is now held as a hypothesis with an experiment
attached), and `briefing.describe`'s compaction rationale, which credited na-373 for something
na-vbe actually measured.

## The spend decision is unchanged and still a human's

4 decisions x 2 arms x 10 runs = 80 calls at $0.088 measured = ~$7. At the measured ~1-in-3
citation rate that yields roughly 25-30 pooled citations, which is thin — `score` says so itself
and prints the n that would settle the observed gap, rather than leaving the reader to work it
out.

What HAS changed: the $7 now buys a measurement rather than a debugging session. Arms, pin,
scorer and controls all run today for free, and the scorer has been shown to recover four
answers known in advance. My recommendation is to spend it — but I have not, and the bead stays
open with the recorded status of ranking still "unmeasured".
